subject: math
title: Geometry I: Perimeter, Area, Circles, Composite Figures, and the Pythagorean Theorem
objectives: You will find the perimeter of rectangles, squares, and other polygons, and tell perimeter apart from area in real-world problems.
You will find the area of rectangles, squares, triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids, choosing the right formula from the GED formula sheet.
You will find the circumference and area of a circle from its radius, diameter, or circumference, using 3.14 or the π key as directed.
You will find the area and perimeter of composite figures by adding or subtracting simple shapes.
You will use the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side of a right triangle and to decide whether a triangle is a right triangle.

slides.title: Week 5 Math: Geometry I
slides.board:
Geometry I

Perimeter, Area, Circles, Composite Figures, and the Pythagorean Theorem

  • Tell perimeter from area and find both
  • Find the area of triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids
  • Find the circumference and area of a circle
  • Break composite figures into simple shapes
  • Use a2 + b2 = c2 for right triangles

Today: warm-up, five concepts with examples, practice together, practice alone, GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 5. Today we measure flat shapes: how far it is around them and how much space they cover. This is everyday math (fencing, flooring, paint, a ladder against a wall) and it shows up all over the GED math test. Every formula we use today is on the GED formula sheet, so the real skill is knowing which formula a problem needs and which measurements go into it. Keep paper and a calculator ready, and sketch every problem as we go.
ask: Have you ever had to buy fencing, carpet, or paint for a room? How did you figure out how much to buy? (expected answer: any; connect fencing to "around" and carpet or paint to "cover")
notes.watch: Pacing for 60 minutes: warm-up 4 min (slide 2); perimeter and area of rectangles 7 min (slides 3–5); other polygons 8 min (slides 6–9); circles 10 min (slides 10–15); composite figures 10 min (slides 16–20); Pythagorean theorem 14 min (slides 21–26); strategy and recap 7 min (slides 27–28). If you fall behind, cut one problem from each we-do slide.

Take about three minutes, then read me your answers. Notice how much multiplying and dividing is in these; we will lean on the same arithmetic today.

For number 4, what is the total number of chips? (expected answer: 10)

notes.say: Perimeter is a walk around the edge, so it is a length: feet, meters, inches. Area is how much surface the shape covers, so it is counted in squares: square feet, square meters. Picture a 4-by-3 rectangle on grid paper; you can count 12 little squares inside, which is 4 times 3. The formulas are on the formula sheet, but the sheet will not tell you whether a question wants perimeter or area. The cue words will.
ask: You are putting a fence around a yard. Perimeter or area? What about grass seed? (expected answer: fence is perimeter; seed is area)
Why is area measured in square units? (expected answer: you are counting how many 1-by-1 squares fit inside)
notes.watch: Students often mix up the units. Ask for the unit with every answer: "52 what?" A missing or wrong unit is a sign they chose the wrong measure.

slides.title: Same Room, Two Questions
slides.board:
A bedroom is 15 feet long and 11 feet wide.

(a) How many feet of baseboard go around the room? (Ignore the door.)

(b) How many square feet of flooring cover the floor?

(c) Flooring costs $3.50 per square foot. What does the flooring cost?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 170' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='68.2,30 231.8,30 231.8,150.0 68.2,150.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='150.0' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>15 ft</text><text x='237.8' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>11 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rectangular bedroom floor 15 ft long and 11 ft wide.

steps: (c) Cost is priced per square foot, so use the area: 165 × $3.50 = $577.50
Same room, two very different numbers. The question decides which one you need.

notes.say: This is the most common setup on the test: one shape, and the question decides whether you need the distance around or the space inside. Baseboard runs along the walls, so it is perimeter. Flooring covers the floor, so it is area. When there is a price, look at what it is priced by: per foot means perimeter, per square foot means area.
ask: What would the flooring cost if someone used the perimeter by mistake? (expected answer: 52 × $3.50 = $182, far too little to cover the floor)
notes.watch: Some students add only one length and one width (26 feet). Have them trace all four walls with a finger and count the sides.

slides.title: Working Backward
slides.board:
(a) A rectangular rug has an area of 96 square feet and a length of 12 feet. What is its perimeter?

(b) A square tile has a perimeter of 36 inches. What is its area?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 170' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='60.0,30 240.0,30 240.0,150.0 60.0,150.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='150.0' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>12 ft</text><text x='246.0' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>w = ?</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rectangular rug 12 ft long with an unknown width w; its area is 96 square feet.

steps: (a) A = lw, so 96 = 12 × w. Divide: w = 96 ÷ 12 = 8 feet
(b) A square has 4 equal sides: s = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 inches

notes.say: Sometimes the GED gives you the answer to one formula and asks for another. Use what you are given to find the missing side first, then use that side in the second formula. Write the formula, put in what you know, and solve for the missing letter.
ask: In part (a), why can't we find the perimeter right away? (expected answer: we do not know the width yet)
notes.watch: A student who answers 8 for part (a) stopped after finding the width. Ask them to reread the question: it asks for the perimeter.

notes.say: A parallelogram is a rectangle that has been pushed over. If you cut the triangle off one end and slide it to the other end, you get a rectangle with the same base and the same height, so the area is base times height. A triangle is half of a parallelogram, which is where the one-half comes from. A trapezoid has one pair of parallel sides, the two bases; you add them, multiply by the height, and take half.
ask: A parallelogram has a base of 10, a slanted side of 6, and a height of 5. What is its area? (expected answer: 50, not 60)
Where does the ½ in the triangle formula come from? (expected answer: a triangle is half of a rectangle or parallelogram with the same base and height)
notes.watch: The slanted side is the number students grab most often. Ask, "Does that side meet the base at a square corner?" If not, it is not the height.

slides.title: Area of Three Shapes
slides.board:
(a) A triangular sail has a base of 8 feet and a height of 12 feet. Find its area.

(b) A garden bed is a trapezoid with parallel sides of 9 m and 15 m. The distance between them is 6 m. Find its area.

(c) A parallelogram has a base of 14 in, a slanted side of 8 in, and a height of 6 in. Find its area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 148' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='40.0,118.0 260.0,118.0 216.0,30 84.0,30' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='84.0' y1='30' x2='84.0' y2='118.0' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='94.0,118.0 94.0,108.0 84.0,108.0' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='150' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>9 m</text><text x='150' y='138.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>15 m</text><text x='90.0' y='79.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>6 m</text></svg>
figure.alt: A trapezoid with a top base of 9 m, a bottom base of 15 m, and a dashed height of 6 m between them.

steps: (b) Add the bases: 9 + 15 = 24. A = ½ × 6 × 24 = 3 × 24 = 72 square meters
(c) Use the height, not the slanted side: A = bh = 14 × 6 = 84 square inches
Traps: 96 for (a) forgets the ½; 112 for (c) uses the slanted side (14 × 8).

notes.say: Write the formula first every time, then put the numbers in. On the triangle, notice that I multiply first and then take half; you can also take half of either number first, whichever is easier. On the parallelogram, the 8-inch side is there to tempt you. It is used for perimeter, never for area.
ask: In part (b), what is the "average base"? (expected answer: 24 ÷ 2 = 12, and 12 × 6 = 72 gives the same area)
notes.watch: For trapezoids, some students multiply all three numbers (9 × 15 × 6). Remind them the bases are added first.

slides.title: Polygons Together
slides.board:
Sketch and label each one first.

  1. A square tile has sides of 9 cm. Find its perimeter and area.
  2. A parallelogram has a base of 15 in, a slanted side of 7 in, and a height of 5 in. Find its area and perimeter.
  3. A triangle has a base of 15 m and a height of 8 m. Find its area.
  4. A trapezoid has bases of 5 ft and 11 ft and a height of 4 ft. Find its area.
steps: 2. A = bh = 15 × 5 = 75 in2; P = 2(15) + 2(7) = 44 in (perimeter uses the slanted side)

notes.say: We will do these together. For each one, tell me the formula before you tell me a number, and I will reveal one line at a time. Number 2 is the important one: the same parallelogram uses the height for area and the slanted side for perimeter.
ask: In number 2, which measurement goes into the area and which goes into the perimeter? (expected answer: height 5 for area; slanted side 7 for perimeter)
In number 4, what do you do first? (expected answer: add the bases, 5 + 11 = 16)
notes.answer: (1) 36 cm and 81 cm<sup>2</sup>   (2) 75 in<sup>2</sup> and 44 in   (3) 60 m<sup>2</sup>   (4) 32 ft<sup>2</sup>
notes.watch: If number 2 comes back as 105 in<sup>2</sup>, the student used the slanted side (15 × 7). If number 3 comes back as 120, the ½ is missing.

slides.title: Your Turn: Polygons
slides.board:
Three minutes. Write the formula, then the answer with units.

  1. A rectangular parking lot is 23 m long and 9 m wide. Find its perimeter.
  2. A triangle has a base of 9 ft and a height of 4 ft. Find its area.
  3. A trapezoid has bases of 10 ft and 16 ft and a height of 7 ft. Find its area.
  4. A rectangle has an area of 72 in2 and a width of 6 in. Find its length.

notes.say: Your turn. I am starting the clock for three minutes. Write the formula you chose next to each problem; that is what I care about most. When time is up, read me your four answers with units.
ask: Read me your four answers with units. (expected answer: 64 m, 18 ft<sup>2</sup>, 91 ft<sup>2</sup>, 12 in)
notes.answer: (1) P = 2(23) + 2(9) = 46 + 18 = 64 m   (2) A = ½ × 9 × 4 = 18 ft<sup>2</sup>   (3) A = ½ × 7 × (10 + 16) = ½ × 7 × 26 = 7 × 13 = 91 ft<sup>2</sup>   (4) 72 = l × 6, so l = 72 ÷ 6 = 12 in
notes.watch: 207 for number 1 is the area (23 × 9). 36 for number 2 forgets the ½. 182 for number 3 forgets the ½. 432 for number 4 multiplied instead of dividing.

slides.title: Circles
slides.board:
• Radius (r): center to edge
  • Diameter (d): all the way across through the center; d = 2r, r = d ÷ 2
  • Circumference (distance around): C = πd = 2πr
  • Area: A = πr2; square the radius first
  • π ≈ 3.14. The question says “use 3.14” or “use the π key” and how to round. Do exactly that.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 185' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='75' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='3' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='75' y1='100' x2='225' y2='100' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='116' y='92' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>diameter d</text><line x1='150' y1='100' x2='195.0' y2='160.0' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='168.5' y='146.5' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>radius r</text></svg>
figure.alt: A circle with its center marked. A diameter crosses the whole circle through the center; a radius runs from the center to the edge.

notes.say: A circle has one key measurement, the radius, and everything else comes from it. The diameter is two radii laid end to end. Circumference is the circle's perimeter, and area is the space inside. Both formulas are on the formula sheet. Say them out loud with me: "C equals pi d. A equals pi r squared." The area formula needs the radius, so if a problem gives you the diameter, cut it in half before you square.
ask: A circle has a diameter of 18. What number goes into the area formula? (expected answer: the radius, 9)
Which answer is a length and which is in square units, circumference or area? (expected answer: circumference is a length; area is square units)
notes.watch: Students often square the diameter. Show that this makes the area four times too big: (2r)<sup>2</sup> = 4r<sup>2</sup>.

slides.title: A Circular Patio
slides.board:
A circular patio has a diameter of 14 feet. Use 3.14 for π.

(a) What is the distance around the patio?

(b) What is the area of the patio?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 185' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='75' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='3' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='75' y1='100' x2='225' y2='100' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='150' y='92' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>14 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A circle with a diameter of 14 ft drawn through its center.

steps: (a) Distance around = circumference. You have the diameter, so C = πd.
(b) Area needs the radius: r = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 feet, and r<sup>2</sup> = 7 × 7 = 49
Trap: 3.14 × 14<sup>2</sup> = 3.14 × 196 = 615.44 uses the diameter and is four times too large.

notes.say: Read the circle question twice: are you given the radius or the diameter, and does it want the distance around or the space inside? Here we have the diameter, so circumference is one step. For area, I write r = 7 before anything else, then square it, then multiply by 3.14.
ask: What would the circumference be using C = 2πr? (expected answer: 2 × 3.14 × 7 = 43.96, the same)
notes.watch: If a student gets 21.98, they used the radius in C = πd (3.14 × 7). Ask: "Is 14 the radius or the diameter?"

slides.title: Working Backward With Circles
slides.board:
A circular garden needs 31.4 meters of edging to go all the way around it. Use 3.14 for π.

What is the area of the garden?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 205' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='75' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='3' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='100' x2='225' y2='100' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='187.5' y='92' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>r = ?</text><text x='150' y='196' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>C = 31.4 m</text></svg>
figure.alt: A circle with an unknown radius; its circumference is 31.4 m.

steps: Edging around = circumference: C = 31.4. Use C = πd to find the diameter.

notes.say: Here the question gives the circumference and wants the area. You cannot jump straight to area, because area needs the radius. Undo the circumference formula to find the diameter, cut it in half, and then use the area formula. It is the same working-backward idea as the rug.
ask: What is the radius if the circumference is 62.8 and you use 3.14? (expected answer: d = 20, so r = 10)
notes.watch: A common slip is using d = 10 as the radius and getting 314. Have the student write "d =" and "r =" on separate lines.

slides.title: Circles Together
slides.board:
1. A fountain has a radius of 5 m. Using 3.14, find its circumference and its area.
  2. A pizza has a diameter of 16 inches. Using 3.14, find its area.
  3. A clock face has a radius of 4 inches. Using the π key, find its circumference and area, each to the nearest tenth.

notes.say: Let's do these together. For each one, first tell me "radius or diameter?" and "around or inside?" Number 3 uses the π key, which gives a slightly different decimal than 3.14. On the test, follow whichever the question says, because the answer choices are built from it.
ask: In number 2, what is the radius? (expected answer: 8 inches)
In number 3, what did your calculator show before rounding the area? (expected answer: about 50.265)
notes.answer: (1) 31.4 m and 78.5 m<sup>2</sup>   (2) 200.96 in<sup>2</sup>   (3) 25.1 in and 50.3 in<sup>2</sup>
notes.watch: If number 2 comes back as 803.84, the student squared the diameter (3.14 × 256). If number 3 comes back as 50.24, the student used 3.14 instead of the π key.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Area of a Circle
slides.board:
A circular tabletop has a diameter of 36 inches. Using 3.14 for π, what is the area of the tabletop?

A. 113.04 square inches
B. 1,017.36 square inches
C. 4,069.44 square inches
D. 56.52 square inches

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 185' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='75' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='3' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='75' y1='100' x2='225' y2='100' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='150' y='92' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>36 in</text></svg>
figure.alt: A circular tabletop with a diameter of 36 inches drawn through its center.

steps: Eliminate A (113.04): that is 3.14 × 36, the circumference. The question asks for area.
Eliminate D (56.52): that is 3.14 × 18. The radius was found but never squared.
Eliminate C (4,069.44): that is 3.14 × 362 = 3.14 × 1,296. The diameter was squared instead of the radius.
B (1,017.36) is correct: r = 36 ÷ 2 = 18; r2 = 324; A = 3.14 × 324 = 1,017.36 square inches.

notes.say: Here is a real GED-style circle question. Every wrong choice is what you get from one specific mistake: the circumference, forgetting to square, or squaring the diameter. So do your own work first, then use the wrong choices as a list of traps you avoided.
ask: Which choice did you pick, and what number did you square? (expected answer: B; I squared the radius, 18)
notes.watch: If the student chose C, ask them to say the area formula out loud and point to the r. If they chose A, ask whether the question wanted the distance around or the space inside.

slides.title: Your Turn: Circles
slides.board:
Three minutes.

  1. A wheel has a diameter of 20 inches. Using 3.14, find its circumference.
  2. A circle has a radius of 9 cm. Using 3.14, find its area.
  3. A round rug has a diameter of 12 feet. Using the π key, find its area to the nearest tenth.

notes.say: Your turn. Write "r =" on your paper for each problem before you do anything else. When the three minutes are up, tell me your answers and the units.
ask: Read me your three answers with units. (expected answer: 62.8 in, 254.34 cm<sup>2</sup>, 113.1 ft<sup>2</sup>)
notes.answer: (1) C = 3.14 × 20 = 62.8 in   (2) A = 3.14 × 9<sup>2</sup> = 3.14 × 81 = 254.34 cm<sup>2</sup>   (3) r = 6; A = π × 36 ≈ 113.097 → 113.1 ft<sup>2</sup>
notes.watch: 125.6 for number 1 doubled the diameter (2 × 3.14 × 20). 28.26 for number 2 forgot to square (3.14 × 9). 452.4 for number 3 squared the diameter.

slides.title: Composite Figures
slides.board:
A composite figure is built from simple shapes.

  1. Find missing sides from the sides you know (opposite sides of a rectangle are equal).
  2. Area: split into pieces and add, or take a big shape and subtract the missing piece.
  3. Perimeter: trace the outside edge only. Lines you draw to split the figure do not count.

Half-circle: area = ½πr2; curved edge = ½πd

figure.alt: An L-shaped figure split by a dashed line into two rectangles.

notes.say: Real shapes are rarely a single rectangle. An L-shaped room, a window with an arched top, a yard with a shed in it: these are composite figures. The plan is always the same. Fill in any missing side lengths, then either add the pieces or subtract the hole. For perimeter, trace the outside with your finger and add only what you touch.
ask: A yard has a shed in it. To find the grass area, do you add or subtract the shed? (expected answer: subtract)
When you split an L-shape with a line, does that line count toward the perimeter? (expected answer: no, it is inside the shape)
notes.watch: Students often count the dividing line in the perimeter, or count an overlap twice in the area. Have them shade each piece a different color once.

slides.title: An L-Shaped Room
slides.board:
An L-shaped room has all right angles. Going clockwise from the top-left corner, its sides are: 6 ft (top), 7 ft (down), 10 ft (right), 5 ft (down), 16 ft (bottom), 12 ft (left).

Find the area and the perimeter.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 195' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='56.7,30.0 126.7,30.0 126.7,111.7 243.3,111.7 243.3,170.0 56.7,170.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='91.7' y='22.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>6 ft</text><text x='132.7' y='75.8' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>7 ft</text><text x='185.0' y='103.7' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>10 ft</text><text x='249.3' y='145.8' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>5 ft</text><text x='150.0' y='190.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>16 ft</text><text x='50.7' y='105.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>12 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: An L-shaped room with right angles. Clockwise from the top-left corner: top 6 ft, down 7 ft, right 10 ft, down 5 ft, bottom 16 ft, left side 12 ft.

steps: Check the sides: top 6 + 10 = 16 matches the bottom; 7 + 5 = 12 matches the left side.
Subtract: full rectangle 16 × 12 = 192; missing top-right corner 10 × 7 = 70; 192 − 70 = 122 ft2

notes.say: Draw this one as I read the sides, starting top left and going clockwise. I like to check the sides first, because the horizontal pieces on top must add up to the bottom, and the vertical pieces on the right must add up to the left side. Then I find the area two ways. When both methods agree, I know I am right.
ask: What is the perimeter of the full 16-by-12 rectangle? (expected answer: 56 ft, the same as the L; cutting a corner out of a rectangle this way does not change the perimeter)
notes.watch: A student who answers 192 forgot to remove the corner. A student who answers 262 added the corner instead of subtracting it.

slides.title: A Rug With a Rounded End
slides.board:
A rug is a rectangle 10 m long and 6 m wide with a half-circle attached to one 6-m end (the 6-m end is the half-circle's diameter). Use the π key and round to the nearest tenth.

Find the area and the perimeter of the rug.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 146' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 45.0 30 L 206.5 30 A 48.5 48.5 0 0 1 206.5 126.9 L 45.0 126.9 L 45.0 30 Z' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='206.5' y1='30' x2='206.5' y2='126.9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='125.8' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>10 m</text><text x='200.5' y='83.5' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>6 m</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rug made of a rectangle 10 m long and 6 m wide with a half-circle attached to its right 6 m end; a dashed line marks where they join.

steps: Area. Rectangle: 10 × 6 = 60 m2. Half-circle: r = 3, so ½ × π × 32 = 4.5π ≈ 14.137 m2
Perimeter. Straight edges: 10 + 10 + 6 = 26 m (the attached 6-m end is inside the rug and does not count).

notes.say: This is the classic GED composite: a rectangle plus half a circle. For area, find the whole circle's area and cut it in half. For perimeter, the curved edge is half of the circumference, and the straight side where the half-circle attaches disappears inside the shape. Round only at the very end.
ask: Why do we add only one 6-m end to the perimeter? (expected answer: the other 6-m end is covered by the half-circle, so it is not on the outside edge)
notes.watch: Watch for 41.4 m: that counts both 6-m ends. Also watch for 88.3 m<sup>2</sup>, which adds a whole circle instead of half.

slides.title: Composite Figures Together
slides.board:
1. A wall is 12 ft wide and 8 ft tall. It has a door 3 ft wide and 7 ft tall. How many square feet of wall need paint?
  2. A backyard is 40 ft by 25 ft. A patio 10 ft by 12 ft sits in it. How many square feet are left for grass?
  3. A stage is a rectangle 20 ft by 12 ft with a half-circle on one 12-ft side. Using 3.14, find the stage's area.

notes.say: Together now. For each one, first tell me: are we adding pieces or subtracting a hole? Then we compute. Number 3 has a half-circle, so say the radius out loud before we do anything.
ask: Add or subtract in number 1? (expected answer: subtract the door)
In number 3, what is the radius of the half-circle? (expected answer: 6 ft)
notes.watch: For number 3, 353.04 means a whole circle was added (240 + 113.04). 466.08 means the radius was taken as 12 (240 + 226.08).

slides.title: Your Turn: Composite Figures
slides.board:
Four minutes. Sketch each figure.

  1. A 10 m by 10 m square has a 4 m by 3 m rectangle cut out of one corner. Find the remaining area.
  2. A sign is a rectangle 9 in wide and 6 in tall with a triangle on top. The triangle's base is the 9-in top edge and its height is 4 in. Find the area.
  3. A round pool with a radius of 5 ft sits in a yard 20 ft by 15 ft. Using 3.14, how much of the yard is not covered by the pool?

notes.say: Your turn. Four minutes on the clock. Decide add or subtract for each one before you compute. Then read me your answers with units.
ask: Read me your three answers. (expected answer: 88 m<sup>2</sup>, 72 in<sup>2</sup>, 221.5 ft<sup>2</sup>)
notes.answer: (1) 100 − 12 = 88 m<sup>2</sup>   (2) rectangle 9 × 6 = 54; triangle ½ × 9 × 4 = 18; 54 + 18 = 72 in<sup>2</sup>   (3) yard 300; pool 3.14 × 25 = 78.5; 300 − 78.5 = 221.5 ft<sup>2</sup>
notes.watch: 90 for number 2 forgot the ½ on the triangle. 268.6 for number 3 used the circumference (31.4) instead of the area.

slides.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
slides.board:
For a right triangle (one 90° angle):

a2 + b2 = c2

  • a and b are the legs; they form the right angle.
  • c is the hypotenuse: across from the right angle, always the longest side.
  • Find c: square, add, square root.
  • Find a leg: square, subtract, square root.

Triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 6-8-10

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='66.7,20 66.7,160.0 253.3,160.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='76.7,160.0 76.7,150.0 66.7,150.0' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='60.7' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>a (leg)</text><text x='160.0' y='180.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>b (leg)</text><text x='170.0' y='86.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>c (hypotenuse)</text></svg>
figure.alt: A right triangle with the right angle at the bottom left. The vertical leg is a, the horizontal leg is b, and the slanted side across from the right angle is c, the hypotenuse.

notes.say: This theorem only works for right triangles. The two sides that make the square corner are the legs; the side across from the corner is the hypotenuse, and it is always the longest. The formula sheet gives you a squared plus b squared equals c squared, but it does not tell you which side is c. Label c first, every time. If c is the unknown, you add. If c is given, you subtract.
ask: A ladder leans against a wall. Which side is the hypotenuse: the wall, the ground, or the ladder? (expected answer: the ladder, across from the right angle where wall meets ground)
Why must the hypotenuse be the longest side? (expected answer: it is across from the largest angle, the 90° angle)
notes.watch: Students who add when they should subtract get a "leg" longer than the hypotenuse. Teach the check: if the answer is longer than the hypotenuse, something is wrong.

slides.title: A TV Screen and a Ladder
slides.board:
(a) A TV screen is 32 inches wide and 24 inches tall. TVs are sold by the length of the diagonal. What is the diagonal?

(b) A 17-foot ladder leans against a wall with its base 8 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='122.7,20 122.7,160.0 197.3,160.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='132.7,160.0 132.7,150.0 122.7,150.0' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='116.7' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>wall ?</text><text x='160.0' y='180.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>8 ft</text><text x='170.0' y='86.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>ladder 17 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A ladder leaning against a wall forms a right triangle: the ground from the wall to the ladder base is 8 ft, the ladder is 17 ft, and the height on the wall is unknown.

steps: (a) The diagonal is the hypotenuse: 32<sup>2</sup> + 24<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup>
(b) The ladder is the hypotenuse (c = 17); 8 is a leg. 8<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> = 17<sup>2</sup>
64 + b2 = 289, so b2 = 289 − 64 = 225, and b = √225 = 15 feet
Check: adding in (b) gives √353 ≈ 18.8 ft, taller than the ladder itself. Impossible.

notes.say: In part (a), the two sides of the screen meet at a right angle and the diagonal is across from it, so we add. In part (b), the ladder is across from the right angle where the wall meets the ground, so the ladder is c and we subtract. Always check that the hypotenuse came out longest.
ask: What would you get in part (b) if you just subtracted 17 − 8? (expected answer: 9, which skips squaring; the right answer is 15)
notes.watch: Students sometimes forget the square root and report 1,600 or 225. Ask: "Is that a length or a length squared?"

slides.title: Right Triangle or Not? Distance on a Grid
slides.board:
(a) Is a triangle with sides 10, 24, and 26 a right triangle?

(b) Is a triangle with sides 7, 9, and 12 a right triangle?

(c) Find the distance between the points (1, 2) and (7, 10).
steps: (a) Longest side is c = 26. 102 + 242 = 100 + 576 = 676, and 262 = 676. Equal, so yes.
(c) Draw a right triangle: horizontal leg 7 − 1 = 6, vertical leg 10 − 2 = 8.

notes.say: The theorem also works in reverse. If the two shorter sides squared and added equal the longest side squared, the triangle is a right triangle; if not, it is not. On a coordinate grid, the straight-line distance between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical distances.
ask: In part (b), would 7 + 9 = 16 tell us anything? (expected answer: no; the test uses squares, not the sides themselves)
notes.watch: Some students test with the wrong side as c. The longest side always goes alone on the right side of the equation.

slides.title: Pythagorean Theorem Together
slides.board:
1. A right triangle has legs of 7 and 24. Find the hypotenuse.
  2. A wire runs from the top of a 12-ft pole to a point on the ground 5 ft from the pole. How long is the wire?
  3. A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 10 and one leg of 6. Find the other leg.
  4. A park is a rectangle 80 m by 60 m. How much shorter is it to walk diagonally across than along two sides?
steps: 4. Two sides: 80 + 60 = 140 m. Diagonal: 6,400 + 3,600 = 10,000; √10,000 = 100 m. Difference: 40 m

notes.say: Together: for each problem, tell me first whether c is known or unknown, and that tells us add or subtract. Number 4 has two steps; read the question carefully, because it asks how much shorter, not how long the diagonal is.
ask: In number 3, add or subtract? Why? (expected answer: subtract, because the hypotenuse is given)
In number 4, what does the question actually ask for? (expected answer: the difference between 140 m and the diagonal)
notes.watch: For number 4, 100 is a stop-one-step-early answer. For number 3, 11.7 comes from adding (√136).

slides.title: Your Turn: Right Triangles
slides.board:
Four minutes.

  1. A right triangle has legs of 15 and 20. Find the hypotenuse.
  2. A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 13 and a leg of 12. Find the other leg.
  3. Is a triangle with sides 5, 6, and 8 a right triangle?
  4. A right triangle has legs of 4 and 7. Find the hypotenuse to the nearest tenth.

notes.say: Your turn, four minutes. Label c first on each one. On number 4 the answer is not a whole number, so you will need the square root key: on the TI-30XS, that is 2nd and then the x-squared key.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: 25, 5, no, 8.1)
notes.watch: 17.7 for number 2 means the student added (√313). 35 for number 1 means the legs were added without squaring.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: The Ladder
slides.board:
A 25-foot ladder leans against a building. The base of the ladder is 7 feet from the building, and the ground is level. How high up the building does the top of the ladder reach?

A. 18 feet
B. 24 feet
C. 25.96 feet
D. 32 feet

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='139.6,20 139.6,160.0 180.4,160.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='149.6,160.0 149.6,150.0 139.6,150.0' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='133.6' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>height ?</text><text x='160.0' y='180.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>7 ft</text><text x='170.0' y='86.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>ladder 25 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A 25 ft ladder leaning against a building forms a right triangle; the base of the ladder is 7 ft from the building and the height reached is unknown.

steps: Eliminate D (32 ft): that is 25 + 7. The sides were added without squaring.
Eliminate A (18 ft): that is 25 − 7. Subtracting is right, but you must subtract the squares.
Eliminate C (25.96 ft): that is √(625 + 49). The squares were added, which makes the wall height longer than the 25-ft ladder. Impossible.
B (24 ft) is correct: the ladder is the hypotenuse. 252 − 72 = 625 − 49 = 576, and √576 = 24 feet.

notes.say: Same setup as our example, new numbers. Before you compute anything, label the hypotenuse. Then look at the choices: two of them come from never squaring, and one comes from adding the squares. Only one is shorter than the ladder and makes sense.
ask: Which side is c, and did you add or subtract? (expected answer: the ladder, 25; subtract)
notes.answer: B. 625 − 49 = 576; √576 = 24 feet. (7-24-25 is a Pythagorean triple.)
notes.watch: If the student chose C, draw the picture and ask whether the top of a 25-ft ladder can be almost 26 ft high.

slides.title: GED Strategy: Sketch, Label, Choose, Check
slides.board:
1. Sketch and label every problem, even when a figure is given.
  2. Decide the question: around (perimeter), inside (area), or a missing side of a right triangle?
  3. Find the formula on the formula sheet and write it before any numbers.
  4. Follow directions for π (3.14 or the π key) and rounding.
  5. Check units and size: ft vs. ft2; the hypotenuse is longest.

notes.say: Most geometry mistakes on the GED are not arithmetic. They come from answering the wrong question, like giving the perimeter when area was asked, or putting the wrong measurement into the right formula. Thirty seconds of sketching and labeling prevents that. The formula sheet is there for you on the whole math test, so use it to confirm the formula, and practice with it this week so you know where each formula sits. On the TI-30XS, use the π key when told to, and the square root is 2nd, then the x-squared key.
ask: A question says "Use 3.14 for π." What happens if you use the π key instead? (expected answer: you may get a slightly different number that does not match the choices)
notes.watch: Some students skip the sketch because a figure is given. Insist on labeling r or h on their own paper: that is where the radius-diameter and height-slant mistakes get caught.

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
• Perimeter = around (ft); area = inside (ft2). Read the cue words.
  • Triangle ½bh, parallelogram bh, trapezoid ½h(b1 + b2). Height meets the base at a right angle.
  • Circle: C = πd, A = πr2. Use the radius for area.
  • Composite: add pieces or subtract holes; perimeter is the outside edge only.
  • a2 + b2 = c2: add to find c, subtract to find a leg.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A → Exit Check

notes.say: That is the whole lesson in five lines. Tell me which one feels strongest and which one you want to practice more. Next, work through the Student Lesson; every screen has a check you answer before moving on. Then do Practice Set A. If you score under 80 percent, take Set B, which has different questions on the same skills. Finish with the Exit Check; passing is 6 out of 8. And remember this week's Practice GED covers the whole math test.
ask: Tell me one mistake from today you will watch for. (expected answer: any, for example "use the radius, not the diameter, for area")

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
This lesson is about measuring flat shapes: the distance around them and the space inside them. You will learn to:

  • find perimeter and area of rectangles and squares, and tell which one a question wants
  • find the area of triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids
  • find the circumference and area of circles
  • break composite figures into simple shapes
  • use the Pythagorean theorem with right triangles

Every formula here is on the GED formula sheet. The sheet will not tell you which formula a problem needs or which measurement goes where. That is what you will practice. Keep paper, a pencil, and a calculator nearby, and sketch every problem.

screens.title: Perimeter: The Distance Around
screens.html:
Perimeter is the total length of all the sides of a figure. Add every side. Because perimeter is a length, its units are plain units: inches, feet, meters.

  • Rectangle: P = 2l + 2w (two lengths and two widths)
  • Square: P = 4s
  • Any other polygon: add all the sides.

Cue words: fence, border, trim, frame, edging, and “around” usually mean perimeter.

example.prompt: A picture frame is 20 inches tall and 16 inches wide. How many inches of trim go around it?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 170' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='102.0,30 198.0,30 198.0,150.0 102.0,150.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='150.0' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>16 in</text><text x='204.0' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>20 in</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rectangular picture frame 16 inches wide and 20 inches tall.

steps: Trim goes around, so find the perimeter: P = 2(20) + 2(16).

check.prompt: A rectangular dog run is 14 feet long and 9 feet wide. How many feet of fencing are needed to go all the way around it?

mistakes.why: That is 14 × 9, the area in square feet. Fencing goes around the edge, so add the sides: 14 + 9 + 14 + 9 = 46.
You added one length and one width. A rectangle has four sides: 2(14) + 2(9) = 28 + 18 = 46.

check.hint: Fencing goes around the edge. A rectangle has two lengths and two widths.
check.explain:
Fencing goes around, so find the perimeter.

P = 2l + 2w = 2(14) + 2(9) = 28 + 18 = 46 feet

If you got 126, you found the area (14 × 9). Area tells how much ground is inside the run, not how much fence surrounds it.

screens.title: Area and Square Units
screens.html:
Area is the amount of surface inside a figure. It is measured in square units: square inches (in2), square feet (ft2), square meters (m2). One square foot is a square 1 foot on each side.

A 4 ft by 3 ft rectangle holds 4 rows of 3 squares: 12 square feet. That is why area is length times width.

  • Rectangle: A = lw
  • Square: A = s2 (side times side)

Cue words: carpet, flooring, paint, tile, sod, and “cover” usually mean area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 170' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='70.0,30 230.0,30 230.0,150.0 70.0,150.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='110.0' y1='30' x2='110.0' y2='150.0' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1'/><line x1='150.0' y1='30' x2='150.0' y2='150.0' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1'/><line x1='190.0' y1='30' x2='190.0' y2='150.0' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1'/><line x1='70.0' y1='70.0' x2='230.0' y2='70.0' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1'/><line x1='70.0' y1='110.0' x2='230.0' y2='110.0' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1'/><text x='150.0' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>4 ft</text><text x='236.0' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>3 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rectangle 4 ft long and 3 ft wide divided into a grid of 12 one-foot squares.

example.prompt: A square tile measures 9 cm on each side. What is its area?

check.prompt: A rectangular living room floor is 18 feet long and 13 feet wide. How many square feet of carpet are needed to cover the floor?

mistakes.why: That is the perimeter, 2(18) + 2(13). Carpet covers the floor, so multiply: 18 × 13 = 234 square feet.
You added the length and width. Area multiplies them: 18 × 13 = 234.

check.hint: Carpet covers the surface. Which formula measures the inside of a rectangle?
check.explain:
Carpet covers the floor, so find the area.

A = lw = 18 × 13 = 234 square feet

(18 × 13 = 18 × 10 + 18 × 3 = 180 + 54 = 234.)

If you got 62, you found the perimeter, which is the distance around the room.

screens.title: Working Backward With Rectangles
screens.html:
Some questions give you the area or perimeter and ask for something else. Use the formula you are given to find the missing side, then use that side in the next formula.

  1. Write the formula you know: A = lw or P = 2l + 2w.
  2. Put in the numbers you have.
  3. Solve for the missing side (undo multiplication by dividing).
  4. Use that side to answer the actual question.

Do not stop after finding the missing side. Reread what the question asks for.

example.prompt: A rectangular rug has an area of 96 square feet and a length of 12 feet. What is its perimeter?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 170' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='60.0,30 240.0,30 240.0,150.0 60.0,150.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='150.0' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>12 ft</text><text x='246.0' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>w = ?</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rectangular rug 12 ft long with an unknown width w; its area is 96 square feet.

check.prompt: A rectangular patio has an area of 168 square feet. Its width is 12 feet. What is the perimeter of the patio?

mistakes.why: That is the length. You found the missing side correctly but stopped there. The question asks for the perimeter: 2(14) + 2(12) = 52.
You added one length and one width (14 + 12). The perimeter has two of each: 2(14) + 2(12) = 52.

check.hint: Use A = lw to find the length first. Then use the perimeter formula.
check.explain:
Find the length: 168 = l × 12, so l = 168 ÷ 12 = 14 feet.

Perimeter: P = 2(14) + 2(12) = 28 + 24 = 52 feet

The most tempting wrong answer is 14, which is only the first step.

screens.title: Area of a Triangle
screens.html:
Draw a diagonal across a rectangle and you get two identical triangles. So a triangle's area is half of a rectangle's:

A = ½bh (half of base times height)

The height is the straight up-and-down distance from the base to the opposite corner. It meets the base at a right angle (90°). In a diagram, look for a dashed line or a small square in the corner. The height is often not one of the sides.

You can multiply b × h and then take half, or take half of either number first, whichever is easier.

example.prompt: A triangular flag has a base of 18 inches and a height of 10 inches. Find its area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 172' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='40.0,142.2 260.0,142.2 117.0,20' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='117.0' y1='20' x2='117.0' y2='142.2' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='127.0,142.2 127.0,132.2 117.0,132.2' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='150.0' y='162.2' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>18 in</text><text x='123.0' y='86.1' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>10 in</text></svg>
figure.alt: A triangle with a base of 18 inches and a dashed height of 10 inches drawn from the top corner straight down to the base.

check.prompt: A triangle has a base of 16 cm and a height of 7 cm. What is its area in square centimeters?

mistakes.why: You multiplied 16 × 7 and stopped. A triangle is half of a rectangle, so take half: 112 ÷ 2 = 56.
You added the base and height. Area multiplies: ½ × 16 × 7 = 56.

check.hint: A = ½bh. Do not forget the half.
check.explain:
A = ½bh = ½ × 16 × 7

16 × 7 = 112, and half of 112 is 56 square centimeters.

If you got 112, you found the area of the rectangle around the triangle.

screens.title: Parallelograms and Height
screens.html:
A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. Cut the triangle off one end, slide it to the other end, and you have a rectangle with the same base and height. So:

A = bh

The height is the perpendicular distance between the bases, not the slanted side. The slanted side is used only for perimeter.

A parallelogram with base 10, slanted side 6, and height 5 has area 10 × 5 = 50, not 10 × 6 = 60. Its perimeter is 2(10) + 2(6) = 32.

check.prompt: The figure shows a parallelogram with a base of 15 m, a slanted side of 9 m, and a height (dashed) of 8 m. What is its area?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 146' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='35.0,116.2 215.4,116.2 265.0,20 84.6,20' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='84.6' y1='20' x2='84.6' y2='116.2' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='94.6,116.2 94.6,106.2 84.6,106.2' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='125.2' y='136.2' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>15 m</text><text x='53.8' y='73.1' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>9 m</text><text x='90.6' y='80.1' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>8 m</text></svg>

why: You used the slanted side as the height (15 × 9). The height is the dashed line that meets the base at a right angle: 15 × 8 = 120.
You took half, which is the triangle formula. A parallelogram is a full rectangle rearranged: A = bh = 15 × 8 = 120.
That is 2(15) + 2(9), the perimeter, and it is in meters, not square meters. Area uses the base and height: 15 × 8 = 120.
check.hint: Which measurement meets the base at a right angle?
check.explain:
A = bh, where h is the perpendicular height.

A = 15 × 8 = 120 square meters

The 9 m slanted side is a distractor for area; it is used only when you find the perimeter (2(15) + 2(9) = 48 m).

screens.title: Area of a Trapezoid
screens.html:
A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides. Those two sides are the bases, b1 and b2. The height is the perpendicular distance between them.

A = ½h(b1 + b2)

In words: add the two bases, multiply by the height, and take half. Another way to think about it: average the two bases, then multiply by the height.

example.prompt: A section of deck is a trapezoid with parallel sides of 10 ft and 16 ft. The distance between them is 7 ft. Find its area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 156' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='40.0,126.2 260.0,126.2 218.8,30 81.2,30' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='81.2' y1='30' x2='81.2' y2='126.2' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><polyline points='91.2,126.2 91.2,116.2 81.2,116.2' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='150' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>10 ft</text><text x='150' y='146.2' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>16 ft</text><text x='87.2' y='83.1' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>7 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A trapezoid with a top base of 10 ft, a bottom base of 16 ft, and a dashed height of 7 ft.

check.prompt: A trapezoid has bases of 8 inches and 14 inches and a height of 5 inches. What is its area in square inches?

mistakes.why: You forgot the ½. 5 × (8 + 14) = 110, and half of that is 55.
You multiplied all three numbers (8 × 14 × 5). The bases are added first: ½ × 5 × (8 + 14) = 55.

check.hint: Add the two bases first. Then multiply by the height and take half.
check.explain:
A = ½h(b1 + b2) = ½ × 5 × (8 + 14)

8 + 14 = 22, and 5 × 22 = 110.

Half of 110 is 55 square inches.

If you got 110, you left out the ½.

screens.title: Radius, Diameter, and Circumference
screens.html:
The radius (r) goes from the center of a circle to its edge. The diameter (d) goes all the way across through the center, so d = 2r and r = d ÷ 2.

The distance around a circle is its circumference. For every circle, the circumference divided by the diameter is the same number, π (pi), about 3.14.

C = πd or C = 2πr (the same thing, because 2r = d)

Circumference is a length, so its units are plain units: inches, feet, meters.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 185' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='75' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='3' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='75' y1='100' x2='225' y2='100' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='116' y='92' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>diameter d</text><line x1='150' y1='100' x2='195.0' y2='160.0' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='168.5' y='146.5' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>radius r</text></svg>
figure.alt: A circle with its center marked. A diameter crosses the whole circle through the center; a radius runs from the center to the edge.

example.prompt: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 26 inches. Using 3.14 for π, find its circumference.
steps: You have the diameter, so use C = πd.

check.prompt: A round table has a radius of 3 feet. Using 3.14 for π, what is its circumference?

mistakes.why: You multiplied 3.14 by the radius. C = πd uses the diameter (6 ft), or use C = 2πr: 2 × 3.14 × 3 = 18.84.
That is 3.14 × 3<sup>2</sup>, the area of the table. Circumference is the distance around: 2 × 3.14 × 3 = 18.84.

check.hint: You are given the radius. Use C = 2πr, or double the radius to get the diameter.
check.explain:
C = 2πr = 2 × 3.14 × 3 = 6 × 3.14 = 18.84 feet

Or: d = 2 × 3 = 6, and C = 3.14 × 6 = 18.84.

If you got 9.42, you used the radius where the diameter belongs.

screens.title: Area of a Circle
screens.html:
A = πr2

Square the radius first (r × r), then multiply by π. Area is in square units.

If the problem gives the diameter, cut it in half before you square. Squaring the diameter gives an area four times too big.

Three common slips: using the diameter, forgetting to square (π × r), and finding the circumference when the question asks for area.

example.prompt: A round pizza has a diameter of 16 inches. Using 3.14 for π, find its area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 185' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='75' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='3' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='75' y1='100' x2='225' y2='100' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='150' y='92' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>16 in</text></svg>
figure.alt: A round pizza with a diameter of 16 inches drawn through its center.

check.prompt: A circular rug has a diameter of 12 feet. Using 3.14 for π, what is the area of the rug?

mistakes.why: You squared the diameter (3.14 × 144). The formula uses the radius: r = 6, so A = 3.14 × 36 = 113.04.
That is 3.14 × 12, the circumference. Area uses A = πr<sup>2</sup> = 3.14 × 6<sup>2</sup> = 113.04.
You found the radius but did not square it (3.14 × 6). Square first: 6<sup>2</sup> = 36, and 3.14 × 36 = 113.04.

check.hint: Find the radius first. Then square it and multiply by 3.14.
check.explain:
r = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 feet

r2 = 6 × 6 = 36

A = 3.14 × 36 = 113.04 square feet

Using 12 in the formula gives 452.16, four times the real area.

screens.title: Using the π Key and Rounding
screens.html:
A GED question will say either “use 3.14 for π” or “use the π key on your calculator.” The π key uses a more exact value (3.14159…), so the two methods give slightly different decimals.

  • Follow the direction in the question exactly. The answer choices are built from it.
  • Do every step on the calculator and round only at the end.
  • To round to the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit: 5 or more rounds up.

example.prompt: A circle has a radius of 4 inches. Using the π key, find its area to the nearest tenth.
steps: The calculator shows 50.265…; the hundredths digit is 6, so round up.

check.prompt: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. Using the π key on your calculator, find the area of the circle. Round to the nearest tenth.

mistakes.why: You used 3.14 instead of the π key. The question asks for the π key: π × 49 ≈ 153.938, which rounds to 153.9.
That is 2πr, the circumference. Area is πr<sup>2</sup> = π × 49 ≈ 153.9.
You used the diameter, 14, in place of the radius (π × 196). Use r = 7: π × 49 ≈ 153.9.

check.hint: Square the radius, multiply by π with the π key, then round.
check.explain:
A = πr2 = π × 72 = π × 49

The calculator shows 153.938…

The hundredths digit is 3, so round down: 153.9 square centimeters.

With 3.14 you would get 153.86, which does not follow the question's directions.

screens.title: Working Backward From Circumference
screens.html:
Some questions give the circumference and ask for the area. Area needs the radius, so find it first:

  1. Use C = πd to find the diameter: d = C ÷ π.
  2. Cut the diameter in half to get the radius.
  3. Use A = πr2.

example.prompt: A circular garden needs 31.4 m of edging around it. Using 3.14 for π, find its area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 205' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='75' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='100' r='3' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='150' y1='100' x2='225' y2='100' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='187.5' y='92' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>r = ?</text><text x='150' y='196' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>C = 31.4 m</text></svg>
figure.alt: A circle with an unknown radius; its circumference is 31.4 m.

check.prompt: The circumference of a round tray is 25.12 inches. Using 3.14 for π, what is the area of the tray?

mistakes.why: You used the diameter, 8, as the radius (3.14 × 64). Cut the diameter in half: r = 4, and 3.14 × 16 = 50.24.
You found r = 4 but did not square it (3.14 × 4). Square first: 4<sup>2</sup> = 16, and 3.14 × 16 = 50.24.

check.hint: Divide the circumference by 3.14 to get the diameter. Then find the radius.
check.explain:
Diameter: d = 25.12 ÷ 3.14 = 8 inches

Radius: r = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 inches

Area: A = 3.14 × 42 = 3.14 × 16 = 50.24 square inches

Using 8 as the radius gives 200.96, four times too big.

screens.title: Composite Figures: Adding Pieces
screens.html:
A composite figure is made of two or more simple shapes. One way to find its area is to split it into pieces, find each area, and add.

  1. Sketch the figure and draw lines to split it into rectangles, triangles, or half-circles.
  2. Find any missing side lengths. Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal.
  3. Find each piece's area with its own formula.
  4. Add the pieces. Count each part only once.

example.prompt: A sign is a rectangle 10 in wide and 8 in tall with a triangle on top. The triangle's base is the 10-in top edge and its height is 5 in. Find the area.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 195' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='92.3,72.7 150.0,15 207.7,72.7 207.7,165.0 92.3,165.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='92.3' y1='72.7' x2='207.7' y2='72.7' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='150.0' y1='15' x2='150.0' y2='72.7' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='150.0' y='185.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>10 in</text><text x='213.7' y='123.8' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>8 in</text><text x='144.0' y='66.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>5 in</text></svg>
figure.alt: A sign made of a rectangle 10 inches wide and 8 inches tall with a triangle on top; the triangle has a dashed height of 5 inches.

check.prompt: A garden is made of a square 8 feet on each side and a right triangle attached to one side of the square. The triangle's legs are 8 feet and 6 feet. What is the total area of the garden?

mistakes.why: You forgot the ½ on the triangle (8 × 6 = 48). The triangle is ½ × 8 × 6 = 24, so the total is 64 + 24 = 88.
You subtracted the triangle. It is attached to the square, so its area is added: 64 + 24 = 88.

check.hint: Find the square's area and the triangle's area separately. In a right triangle, the legs are the base and height.
check.explain:
Square: 82 = 64 ft2

Triangle: the legs meet at a right angle, so they are the base and height. ½ × 8 × 6 = 24 ft2

Total: 64 + 24 = 88 square feet

Getting 112 means the triangle was counted as a full rectangle.

screens.title: Composite Figures: Subtracting a Piece
screens.html:
The other way to find a composite area is to start with a big shape and subtract the part that is missing or not included.

  • Grass in a yard = yard − shed.
  • Wall to paint = wall − doors − windows.
  • An L-shape = the full rectangle − the missing corner.

Subtract every hole. A wall with a door and a window needs both removed.

example.prompt: A backyard is a rectangle 30 ft by 20 ft. A shed 8 ft by 5 ft sits in it. How many square feet are covered by grass?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 170' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='60.0,30 240.0,30 240.0,150.0 60.0,150.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='80.0' y='100.0' width='48.0' height='30.0' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><text x='104.0' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>8 ft</text><text x='133.0' y='120.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>5 ft</text><text x='150.0' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>30 ft</text><text x='246.0' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>20 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rectangular backyard 30 ft by 20 ft with a smaller rectangular shed 8 ft by 5 ft inside it.

check.prompt: A wall is 14 feet wide and 9 feet tall. It has a window 4 feet wide and 3 feet tall and a door 3 feet wide and 7 feet tall. How many square feet of wall need paint?

mistakes.why: You subtracted the window but not the door (126 − 12). Remove both: 126 − 12 − 21 = 93.
You subtracted the door but not the window (126 − 21). Remove both: 126 − 21 − 12 = 93.
You added the window and door to the wall. They are holes that get no paint, so subtract them: 126 − 33 = 93.

check.hint: Find the whole wall's area. Then subtract every opening.
check.explain:
Wall: 14 × 9 = 126 ft2

Window: 4 × 3 = 12 ft2. Door: 3 × 7 = 21 ft2.

Paint: 126 − 12 − 21 = 93 square feet

The most common slip is removing only one of the two openings.

screens.title: Perimeter of Composite Figures
screens.html:
For perimeter, trace only the outside edge of the figure. Lines inside the figure, including any lines you drew to split it and any side where two pieces are joined, do not count.

For a half-circle on the edge, the curved part is half of a circumference: ½πd. Two half-circles with the same diameter make one whole circle.

example.prompt: A rug is a rectangle 10 m by 6 m with a half-circle on one 6-m end. Using the π key, find the perimeter to the nearest tenth.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 146' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 45.0 30 L 206.5 30 A 48.5 48.5 0 0 1 206.5 126.9 L 45.0 126.9 L 45.0 30 Z' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='206.5' y1='30' x2='206.5' y2='126.9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='125.8' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>10 m</text><text x='200.5' y='83.5' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>6 m</text></svg>
figure.alt: A rug made of a rectangle 10 m long and 6 m wide with a half-circle attached to its right 6 m end; a dashed line marks where they join.

steps: Straight edges: 10 + 10 + 6 = 26 m. The joined 6-m end is inside the rug.

check.prompt: A tabletop is a rectangle 8 feet long and 4 feet wide with a half-circle on each 4-foot end, as shown. Using 3.14 for π, what is the perimeter of the tabletop?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 116' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M 83.3 30 L 216.7 30 A 33.3 33.3 0 0 1 216.7 96.7 L 83.3 96.7 A 33.3 33.3 0 0 1 83.3 30 Z' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='216.7' y1='30' x2='216.7' y2='96.7' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><line x1='83.3' y1='30' x2='83.3' y2='96.7' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5,4'/><text x='150.0' y='22' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>8 ft</text><text x='210.7' y='68.3' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>4 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A tabletop made of a rectangle 8 ft long and 4 ft wide with a half-circle attached to each 4 ft end. Dashed lines mark where the half-circles meet the rectangle; each dashed line is 4 ft long.

mistakes.why: You also counted the two 4-ft ends (the dashed lines). They are inside the tabletop, so only the two 8-ft sides and the curved edges count: 16 + 12.56 = 28.56.
You counted only one half-circle (6.28). There is one at each end, and together they make a whole circle: 16 + 12.56 = 28.56.

check.hint: Trace the outside edge. The two half-circles together make one whole circle with a diameter of 4 ft.
check.explain:
Straight edges on the outside: 8 + 8 = 16 ft

The two half-circles make one whole circle with d = 4: C = 3.14 × 4 = 12.56 ft

Perimeter: 16 + 12.56 = 28.56 feet

The dashed 4-ft lines are where the pieces join, so they are not part of the edge. Counting them gives 36.56.

screens.title: The Pythagorean Theorem: Finding the Hypotenuse
screens.html:
A right triangle has one 90° angle. The two sides that form the right angle are the legs (a and b). The side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse (c). It is always the longest side.

a2 + b2 = c2

To find the hypotenuse: square each leg, add, then take the square root. On the TI-30XS, the square root is 2nd, then the x2 key.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='66.7,20 66.7,160.0 253.3,160.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='76.7,160.0 76.7,150.0 66.7,150.0' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='60.7' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>a (leg)</text><text x='160.0' y='180.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>b (leg)</text><text x='170.0' y='86.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>c (hypotenuse)</text></svg>
figure.alt: A right triangle with the right angle at the bottom left. The vertical leg is a, the horizontal leg is b, and the side across from the right angle is c, the hypotenuse.

example.prompt: A support wire runs from the top of a 12-ft pole to a point on the ground 5 ft from the bottom of the pole. How long is the wire?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='130.8,20 130.8,160.0 189.2,160.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='140.8,160.0 140.8,150.0 130.8,150.0' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='124.8' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>pole 12 ft</text><text x='160.0' y='180.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>5 ft</text><text x='170.0' y='86.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>wire ?</text></svg>
figure.alt: A 12 ft pole standing straight up, with a wire from its top to a point on the ground 5 ft from its base; the wire length is unknown.

steps: The pole and ground meet at a right angle, so the wire is the hypotenuse.

check.prompt: A right triangle has legs of 8 and 15. How long is the hypotenuse?

mistakes.why: You added the legs without squaring them. Square first: 64 + 225 = 289, then √289 = 17.
That is c<sup>2</sup>. Take the square root to get c: √289 = 17.
You subtracted the squares (√(225 − 64) ≈ 12.7). When you are finding the hypotenuse, add: √(64 + 225) = 17.

check.hint: Square each leg, add, then take the square root.
check.explain:
a2 + b2 = c2

82 + 152 = 64 + 225 = 289

c = √289 = 17

Check: 17 is longer than both legs, as a hypotenuse must be.

screens.title: The Pythagorean Theorem: Finding a Leg
screens.html:
When the hypotenuse is given and a leg is missing, subtract:

leg2 = c2 − (other leg)2, then take the square root.

The key is labeling c correctly. Ask: which side is across from the right angle? A ladder against a wall, a ramp, a wire to the ground, and a diagonal across a rectangle are usually hypotenuses.

Check yourself: a leg must be shorter than the hypotenuse. If your leg comes out longer, you added when you should have subtracted.

example.prompt: A 10-foot ladder leans against a wall with its base 6 feet from the wall. How high does it reach?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 300 190' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polygon points='107.5,20 107.5,160.0 212.5,160.0' fill='#F3E9C9' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='117.5,160.0 117.5,150.0 107.5,150.0' fill='none' stroke='#0A1F3D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='101.5' y='95.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='end'>height ?</text><text x='160.0' y='180.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='middle'>6 ft</text><text x='170.0' y='86.0' font-size='14' fill='#0A1F3D' text-anchor='start'>ladder 10 ft</text></svg>
figure.alt: A 10 ft ladder leaning against a wall with its base 6 ft from the wall; the height it reaches is unknown.

steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse: c = 10, and 6 is a leg.

check.prompt: A 20-foot ladder leans against a wall. The base of the ladder is 12 feet from the wall, and the ground is level. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?

mistakes.why: You added the squares (√(400 + 144) ≈ 23.3). That would put the top of the ladder higher than the ladder is long. The ladder is the hypotenuse, so subtract: √(400 − 144) = 16.
You subtracted the lengths (20 − 12) without squaring. Square first: 400 − 144 = 256, and √256 = 16.

Adding the squares gives about 23.3 ft, which is longer than the ladder. That cannot be right.

screens.title: Is It a Right Triangle?
screens.html:
The Pythagorean theorem also works in reverse. To test whether three side lengths make a right triangle:

  1. Let c be the longest side.
  2. Compute a2 + b2 for the two shorter sides.
  3. If it equals c2 exactly, it is a right triangle. If not, it is not.

Common right-triangle sets (triples): 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and multiples such as 6-8-10.

example.prompt: Is a triangle with sides 6, 7, and 9 a right triangle?
steps: The longest side is 9, so c = 9 and c<sup>2</sup> = 81.
example.answer: No, it is not a right triangle.

check.prompt:
A triangle has sides of 12, 16, and 20. Complete the test.

The sum of the squares of the two shorter sides is 122 + 162 = {{0}}.

That is 12 + 16 without squaring. Square each side first: 144 + 256 = 400.
That is only 16<sup>2</sup>. Add 12<sup>2</sup> too: 144 + 256 = 400.
That is 20 × 2. Squaring means multiplying a number by itself: 20 × 20 = 400.
That is the side itself, not its square. 20<sup>2</sup> = 20 × 20 = 400.

why: The two values match (400 = 400), and when a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> = c<sup>2</sup> exactly, the triangle is a right triangle.
The Pythagorean test uses only the side lengths. Because 12<sup>2</sup> + 16<sup>2</sup> equals 20<sup>2</sup>, it is a right triangle; no angles are needed.

202 = 400

The two values are equal, so the triangle is a right triangle. (It is the 3-4-5 triangle times 4.)

screens.title: Right Triangles in Real Life
screens.html:
Look for hidden right triangles. A diagonal across a rectangle (a TV screen, a field, a door) splits it into two right triangles, with the diagonal as the hypotenuse. A shortcut across a corner is the hypotenuse; walking along the two sides is the legs.

On a coordinate grid, the straight-line distance between two points is a hypotenuse. The legs are the horizontal distance (difference in x) and the vertical distance (difference in y).

example.prompt: Find the distance between the points (1, 2) and (7, 10).

check.prompt: A computer monitor screen is 48 centimeters wide and 36 centimeters tall. Screens are measured along the diagonal. What is the diagonal length of this screen?

You subtracted the squares. The diagonal is across from the right corner of the screen, so it is the hypotenuse: add the squares. √3,600 = 60.

The width and height are the legs; the diagonal is the hypotenuse.

√3,600 = 60 centimeters

(This is the 3-4-5 triangle times 12.)

screens.title: Choosing the Right Formula
screens.html:
On the GED, the formula sheet lists the formulas. Your job is to pick the right one. Ask three questions:

  1. Around, inside, or a missing side? Around means perimeter or circumference. Inside means area. A missing side of a right triangle means the Pythagorean theorem.
  2. What shape? Rectangle, triangle, parallelogram, trapezoid, circle, or a mix.
  3. Which measurements? Height, not the slanted side, for area. Radius, not diameter, for circle area.

Then check the units: feet for perimeter, square feet for area.

check.prompt: A homeowner wants to put a wallpaper border along the top of all four walls of a rectangular room that is 12 feet long and 10 feet wide. Which calculation gives the length of border needed?
why: That is the area of the floor (120 square feet). A border runs around the room, which is a length: the perimeter.
That is the area of a triangle with base 12 and height 10. A border runs around all four walls, so add the sides: 2(12) + 2(10).
That is the length of the diagonal across the floor, from the Pythagorean theorem. A border follows the walls, so it is the perimeter.
check.hint: Does a border go around the room or cover the floor?
check.explain:
A border runs along the walls, all the way around the room. That is the perimeter.

P = 2(12) + 2(10) = 24 + 20 = 44 feet.

12 × 10 would give the floor area in square feet, which solves a different problem.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Perimeter = distance around (units: ft, m). Rectangle P = 2l + 2w; square P = 4s; otherwise add every side.
  • Area = surface inside (units: ft2, m2). Rectangle lw; square s2; triangle ½bh; parallelogram bh; trapezoid ½h(b1 + b2).
  • Height meets the base at a right angle; a slanted side is not the height.
  • Circles: d = 2r; C = πd = 2πr; A = πr2. Use the radius for area. Follow the directions for 3.14 or the π key.
  • Composite figures: add the pieces or subtract the holes. Perimeter counts the outside edge only.
  • Pythagorean theorem: a2 + b2 = c2. Add the squares to find c; subtract to find a leg. The hypotenuse is always the longest side.

Next: Practice Set A. Sketch every problem and write the formula before the numbers.

items.prompt: Dana wants to put a fence around all four sides of a rectangular garden that is 18 feet long and 12 feet wide. How many feet of fencing does she need?
why: You added one length and one width (18 + 12), which is only half of the way around. A rectangle has two lengths and two widths: 2(18) + 2(12) = 60.
That is 18 × 12, the area of the garden in square feet. Fencing goes around the edge, so add the four sides.
That is 4 × 18, which treats the garden as a square with every side 18 feet. Two of the sides are only 12 feet: 2(18) + 2(12) = 60.
items.hint: Fencing goes around the edge, so add all four sides: two lengths and two widths.
items.explain:
Fencing goes around the garden, so find the perimeter.

P = 2l + 2w = 2(18) + 2(12)

2(18) = 36 and 2(12) = 24

36 + 24 = 60 feet

The choice 30 feet adds only one length and one width (half the perimeter). The choice 216 feet is 18 × 12, the area in square feet, which solves a different problem. The choice 72 feet treats the garden as a square with sides of 18.

items.prompt: A triangular road sign has a base of 30 inches and a height of 26 inches. What is the area of the sign in square inches?

mistakes.why: You multiplied 30 × 26 and stopped. A triangle is half of a rectangle with the same base and height: 780 ÷ 2 = 390.
You added the base and height. Area multiplies them and takes half: ½ × 30 × 26 = 390.

items.hint: Use A = ½bh. Take half of the base first to make the arithmetic easier.
items.explain:
A = ½bh = ½ × 30 × 26

Half of 30 is 15, and 15 × 26 = 390.

The area is 390 square inches.

The most tempting wrong answer is 780, which leaves out the ½.

items.prompt: A circular rug has a diameter of 10 feet. Binding tape will be sewn around the entire edge of the rug. Using 3.14 for π, how many feet of binding tape are needed?

mistakes.why: That is 3.14 × 5<sup>2</sup>, the area of the rug in square feet. Tape goes around the edge, so use C = πd = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4.
You used 2π with the diameter (2 × 3.14 × 10). The 2πr form needs the radius, 5. With the diameter, C = πd = 31.4.
You multiplied 3.14 by the radius, 5. C = πd uses the full diameter: 3.14 × 10 = 31.4.

items.hint: The distance around a circle is the circumference: C = πd. You are given the diameter.
items.explain:
The edge of a circle is its circumference. You know the diameter, so use C = πd.

C = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 feet

A common mistake is to use the area formula: 3.14 × 52 = 78.5, which is the number of square feet the rug covers, not the length of its edge. Another mistake is to double the diameter: 2 × 3.14 × 10 = 62.8. The formula 2πr uses the radius (5), not the diameter.

items.prompt: A lawn sprinkler sprays water 15 feet in every direction, watering a circle with a radius of 15 feet. Using 3.14 for π, how many square feet of lawn does it water?

You used 30 (the diameter) in the area formula: 3.14 × 900. The 15 feet is already the radius, so A = 3.14 × 225 = 706.5.

The water reaches 15 feet from the sprinkler in every direction, so r = 15.

A = πr2 = 3.14 × 152 = 3.14 × 225 = 706.5 square feet

94.2 is the distance around the watered circle, not the space inside it.

The figure shows a parallelogram. Its base is 12 centimeters, its slanted side is 7 centimeters, and its height (the dashed line) is 5 centimeters.

What is the area of the parallelogram?

why: You used the slanted side as the height (12 × 7). The height is the dashed line that meets the base at a right angle: 12 × 5 = 60.

items.prompt:
The side wall of a storage shed is shaped like a trapezoid. Its front edge is 9 feet tall and its back edge is 6 feet tall; both edges are vertical, so they are parallel. The bottom edge between them is 8 feet long and meets both at right angles.

items.prompt: A 13-foot ladder leans against the side of a house. The bottom of the ladder is 5 feet from the base of the wall, and the ground is level. How high up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?

r = 62.8 ÷ 6.28 = 10 feet

items.prompt:

items.prompt: A rectangular picture frame is 24 inches tall and 18 inches wide. How many inches of ribbon are needed to go all the way around the frame?

items.prompt: A triangular piece of fabric has a base of 14 inches and a height of 9 inches. What is the area of the fabric?

A = ½bh = ½ × 14 × 9

½ × 126 = 63 square inches

The choice 126 forgets to take half. The choice 23 adds 14 + 9 instead of multiplying. The choice 31.5 takes half twice.

items.prompt: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 28 inches. When the wheel makes one full turn, the bike moves forward a distance equal to the wheel's circumference. Using 3.14 for π, how far does the bike move in one full turn?

C = πd = 3.14 × 28 = 87.92 inches

175.84 doubles the diameter, a mix-up between the two forms of the formula.

items.prompt: A circular clock face has a radius of 6 inches. What is the area of the clock face? Use the π key on your calculator and round to the nearest tenth of a square inch.

Rounded to the nearest tenth: 113.1 square inches

items.prompt:

why: You used the slanted side as the height (20 × 10). The height is the dashed line that meets the base at a right angle: 20 × 8 = 160.

A = 20 × 8 = 160 square feet

The 10-foot slanted side is used for perimeter, not area. Using it gives 200 square feet, the most tempting wrong choice.

items.prompt: Find the area of each figure. Then drag each figure into the bin that shows its area. All measurements are in units, and heights are perpendicular to the bases.

Triangle (base 16, height 10): ½ × 16 × 10 = 80 → 80 square units

Trapezoid (bases 12 and 8, height 8): ½ × 8 × (12 + 8) = 4 × 20 = 80 → 80 square units

Notice that a triangle and a parallelogram with the same base and height do not have the same area: the triangle is half. Forgetting the ½ would put the first triangle in the 40 bin.

Hypotenuse: 92 + 122 = 81 + 144 = 225, and √225 = 15. (225 is c2, not c; 21 is 9 + 12; 7.9 comes from subtracting: √(144 − 81) = √63 ≈ 7.9.)

vocab.def: The total distance around the outside of a flat figure.

vocab.def: The amount of surface a flat figure covers, measured in square units.

vocab.def: The side of a figure that its height is measured from; in a trapezoid, each of the two parallel sides is a base.

Week 5 Study Sheet: Geometry I

Perimeter (distance around)

  • Add all the sides. Units: ft, m, in.
  • Rectangle: P = 2l + 2w
  • Square: P = 4s
  • Circle (circumference): C = πd = 2πr

Circle Facts

  • d = 2r and r = d ÷ 2
  • π ≈ 3.14 (or use the π key as directed)
  • Area uses the radius: A = πr2

Pythagorean Theorem (right triangles)

a2 + b2 = c2   (c = hypotenuse, the longest side, across from the right angle)

  • Find c: square, add, square root.
  • Find a leg: square, subtract, square root.
  • Triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 6-8-10
  • Is it a right triangle? Check whether a2 + b2 = c2 with the longest side as c.

Top Mistakes

  • Forgetting ½ for triangles and trapezoids
  • Using a slanted side as the height
  • Using the diameter in A = πr2
  • Adding instead of subtracting to find a leg
  • Giving perimeter when area was asked
  • Counting a joined side in a composite perimeter
  • Stopping one step early (width found, perimeter not)
